q: What is the difference between Azure RBAC roles and Microsoft Entra roles, and where does each apply?
p: Azure RBAC controls access to Azure resources (subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, storage) using role assignments at a scope. Entra roles control the identity directory itself: users, groups, apps, Conditional Access. They are separate systems with separate assignment points.
cmds: az role assignment create --assignee <id> --role 'Contributor' --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/app-rg
az role assignment list --assignee <id> --all -o table
az rest --method get --url https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/directoryRoles
tip: Mention the elevate-access toggle for Global Administrators, which is the bridge between the two worlds, and that it should be rare and audited.
a: Azure RBAC governs what a principal can do to Azure resources. A role assignment ties a principal, a role definition such as Reader, Contributor or a custom role, and a scope, which can be a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource, and permissions inherit downward. Microsoft Entra roles govern the directory: creating users and groups, registering applications, managing Conditional Access or resetting passwords. A Global Administrator, for example, does not automatically have rights over subscriptions, though they can elevate themselves, and a subscription Owner has no power in the directory. I keep both models least-privilege: use groups for assignments, scope narrowly, prefer built-in roles, use Privileged Identity Management for time-limited elevation, and review access regularly. When troubleshooting a denied action, I first work out which plane the action belongs to, then look at assignments, deny assignments and Azure Policy.

q: System-assigned versus user-assigned managed identities: when do you use each?
p: A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it. A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to many resources and survives their deletion. Both give tokens without secrets.
cmds: az identity create -g app-rg -n web-uami
az vm identity assign -g app-rg -n vm1 --identities web-uami
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id <principalId> --role 'Storage Blob Data Reader' --scope <storage-id>
tip: User-assigned identities let you pre-create role assignments before the resource exists, which avoids deployment ordering problems.
a: Both kinds of managed identity give an Azure resource an Entra identity so that code can get tokens without storing credentials. A system-assigned identity is created with the resource, has the same lifecycle, and is the simplest choice for a single VM or app that needs access to one thing. A user-assigned identity is created as its own resource, can be shared by multiple resources, and persists if they are replaced. I prefer user-assigned in infrastructure as code because I can create the identity and its role assignments first, then attach it, avoiding race conditions during deployment, and it fits scenarios like scale sets, many instances of the same app, or blue-green swaps. The trade-off is that a shared identity widens the blast radius, so I do not share one across unrelated workloads. On AKS I use Workload Identity federated to a user-assigned identity.

q: Explain Azure Policy effects such as Audit, Deny, Modify and DeployIfNotExists, and how you roll out a new policy safely.
p: Audit flags non-compliance only. Deny blocks the request. Modify adds or changes properties like tags. DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource, such as diagnostic settings, when missing. Assignments can be set to DoNotEnforce first.
cmds: az policy assignment create --name require-tags --policy <def-id> --scope /subscriptions/<sub> --enforcement-mode DoNotEnforce
az policy state list --filter "complianceState eq 'NonCompliant'" -o table
az policy remediation create -n fix-diag --policy-assignment require-diag
tip: Start with Audit or DoNotEnforce, read the compliance data, fix existing resources, then switch to Deny.
a: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules at creation and continuously afterwards. The effect decides the outcome. Audit records a non-compliant event without blocking. Deny rejects the request before the resource is created or changed. Modify can add, replace or remove properties such as tags or settings, using a managed identity. DeployIfNotExists and AuditIfNotExists look for a related resource, for example diagnostic settings or an agent, and deploy it or report it missing. To roll out safely, I assign the policy in Audit or with enforcement mode set to DoNotEnforce, review compliance results, communicate with teams, add exemptions where justified, run remediation tasks for existing resources, and only then switch to Deny. I group related policies into initiatives, assign them at management group level, and manage them as code with testing in a sandbox subscription.

q: How do NSGs, application security groups and service tags work together, and how are rules evaluated?
p: An NSG holds numbered allow and deny rules for a subnet or NIC; the lowest priority number that matches wins. Service tags represent Azure service IP ranges, and application security groups let you write rules by workload role instead of IP address.
cmds: az network nsg rule create -g net-rg --nsg-name web-nsg -n allow-https --priority 100 --access Allow --protocol Tcp --destination-port-ranges 443 --source-address-prefixes Internet
az network watcher show-security-group-view --vm vm1 -g app-rg
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g app-rg --name nic1
tip: Effective security rules and IP flow verify in Network Watcher tell you exactly which rule allowed or blocked a flow.
a: A network security group contains inbound and outbound rules, each with a priority from one hundred to four thousand ninety-six. Azure checks rules from the lowest number upward and stops at the first match. There are default rules at the end that allow VNet and load balancer traffic and deny the rest. NSGs can be attached to a subnet, a network interface, or both, in which case both must allow the traffic. Service tags like Storage, Sql or AzureLoadBalancer stand for Microsoft-managed address ranges that update automatically, so rules do not break when IPs change. Application security groups let me group network interfaces by role, for example web, app and db, and write rules between groups rather than address lists. For troubleshooting I use IP flow verify and effective security rules in Network Watcher, and NSG flow logs for traffic analysis.

q: What do Azure Bastion and just-in-time VM access provide compared with exposing RDP or SSH?
p: Bastion is a managed jump service that gives browser or native-client RDP and SSH over TLS to VMs with only private IPs. Just-in-time access in Defender for Cloud opens management ports on an NSG only for a requested time and source.
cmds: az network bastion create -g net-rg -n hub-bastion --vnet-name hub --public-ip-address bastion-pip --sku Standard
az network bastion ssh --name hub-bastion -g net-rg --target-resource-id <vm-id> --auth-type AAD
tip: The aim is no public IPs and no standing open management ports on any VM.
a: Exposing RDP or SSH to the internet invites constant scanning and brute force attacks. Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS service deployed in a dedicated subnet. Users connect through the Azure portal or a native client over TLS, and Bastion reaches the VM over its private address, so the VM needs no public IP. With the Standard SKU I get native client support, shareable links and Entra ID sign-in, and I can combine it with Conditional Access and recorded sessions through logging. Just-in-time access from Defender for Cloud takes a different approach: management ports stay closed in the NSG, and when someone requests access, a rule is created for their source IP for a limited time, with the request logged and approved through RBAC. I often use Bastion for access and JIT or PIM for authorisation, and for automation I prefer agent-based tools like Run Command.
f: Why does Bastion need its own subnet?
How is JIT approval logged?

q: Azure Virtual WAN versus a traditional hub-and-spoke network: when do you pick each?
p: Hub-and-spoke is a self-managed pattern: a VNet hub with firewall, gateways and peering to spokes. Virtual WAN is a managed hub service that automates routing, branch connectivity and transitive connections at scale, with less manual route work and a higher service cost.
cmds: az network vwan create -g net-rg -n corp-wan --type Standard
az network vhub create -g net-rg -n hub-we --vwan corp-wan --address-prefix 10.100.0.0/23 -l westeurope
az network vhub connection create -g net-rg --vhub-name hub-we -n spoke1 --remote-vnet spoke1-vnet
tip: A fair answer: choose hub-and-spoke for control and a handful of regions, Virtual WAN when you have many branches and regions.
a: In a hub-and-spoke design I build the hub VNet myself with Azure Firewall or a network virtual appliance, VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, and peer each spoke VNet to it, using user-defined routes to force traffic through the firewall. It gives the most control and is cheaper for small estates, but the routing tables, peerings and gateway transit settings become a lot to maintain, especially across regions. Virtual WAN provides a Microsoft-managed hub, called a virtual hub, with built-in routing, automatic any-to-any connectivity between branches and VNets, and integrated VPN, ExpressRoute and firewall options. It reduces manual route management and scales to hundreds of branches, but costs more and has some restrictions on customisation. I pick Virtual WAN for many sites and regions, and traditional hub-and-spoke when requirements are specific or the network is modest.

q: Azure Front Door, Traffic Manager and Application Gateway: how do you choose for global versus regional traffic?
p: Traffic Manager is DNS-based routing with no data path. Front Door is a global Layer 7 edge with CDN, WAF and fast failover. Application Gateway is a regional Layer 7 load balancer with WAF. Combine Front Door in front of regional gateways.
cmds: az afd profile create -g edge-rg --profile-name global --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor
az network traffic-manager profile create -g edge-rg -n tm --routing-method Performance --unique-dns-name myapp-tm
tip: Remember to lock backends to accept traffic only from Front Door, using its service tag and the X-Azure-FDID header.
a: Traffic Manager works at DNS level. It answers queries with the endpoint chosen by priority, weighted, performance or geographic rules, and never sees the traffic, so failover depends on DNS caching and it works for any protocol. Front Door is a global HTTP and HTTPS entry point on Microsoft's edge network, offering anycast, TLS termination, caching, WAF, URL routing and quick health-based failover. Application Gateway is regional, lives inside your VNet, and offers WAF, path routing, session affinity and AKS ingress integration. A common pattern for multi-region applications is Front Door at the edge, with an Application Gateway or internal load balancer per region, and private origins using Private Link. I choose Traffic Manager for non-HTTP workloads or simple DNS routing, and add header validation so users cannot bypass the edge security.

q: System versus user node pools on AKS: why separate them and how do you configure each?
p: System pools host critical add-ons like CoreDNS and metrics-server and must have at least one node. User pools run application workloads. Separating them with a taint on the system pool prevents apps from starving cluster components.
cmds: az aks nodepool add -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -n apps --mode User --node-count 3 --zones 1 2 3
az aks nodepool update -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -n system --node-taints CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule
az aks nodepool list -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -o table
tip: Run at least three system nodes across zones in production, and keep system pools on a stable VM size.
a: AKS supports two node pool modes. System pools host the essential components of the cluster, for instance CoreDNS, konnectivity and metrics-server, and every cluster needs at least one. User pools are where application pods run, and they can scale to zero. I separate them so a runaway application cannot starve cluster components. I apply the CriticalAddonsOnly taint to the system pool so only tolerated pods land there. System pools are sized modestly but kept highly available, with three nodes spread across availability zones, and use a general-purpose VM size. User pools are sized for the workload and I often create several: different VM families for memory-heavy or GPU workloads, Spot pools for tolerant jobs, separate pools per tenant or compliance boundary, each with its own autoscaler settings and upgrade surge configuration.
f: Why can user pools scale to zero but system pools cannot?
How do you upgrade pools independently?

q: How do AKS upgrade channels and node OS image upgrades work, and how do you keep clusters patched safely?
p: Cluster auto-upgrade channels (patch, stable, rapid, node-image) move the Kubernetes version automatically. Node OS upgrade channels apply security patches or new images. Planned maintenance windows and surge settings control when and how fast.
cmds: az aks update -g aks-rg -n prod --auto-upgrade-channel patch --node-os-upgrade-channel NodeImage
az aks maintenanceconfiguration add -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -n aksManagedAutoUpgradeSchedule --schedule-type Weekly --day-of-week Sunday --start-hour 2 --duration 4
az aks nodepool update -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -n apps --max-surge 33%
tip: Roll non-production first with a faster channel so production follows a version that has already survived testing.
a: AKS has two independent upgrade dimensions. The cluster auto-upgrade channel controls the Kubernetes version: patch keeps you on the latest patch of your minor version, stable follows the latest supported minor minus one, rapid takes the newest, and node-image only updates node images. The node OS upgrade channel controls the operating system: Unmanaged leaves patching to you, SecurityPatch applies security updates without reimaging, NodeImage replaces nodes with a fresh image weekly. I configure maintenance windows so changes happen at quiet times, set the max surge on node pools to control speed, and make sure PodDisruptionBudgets and multiple replicas protect workloads during drains. Lower environments use faster channels so problems appear there first. I also monitor for deprecated APIs and keep track of the version support window, which is limited. Skipping upgrades is risky because older versions fall out of support.

q: How does Azure Container Registry support geo-replication, ACR Tasks and secure image pulls from AKS?
p: Premium ACR can replicate a registry to multiple regions behind one login server for faster pulls and resilience. ACR Tasks build and patch images in the cloud. AKS pulls with its kubelet managed identity granted AcrPull, with no passwords.
cmds: az acr replication create -r myacr -l northeurope
az aks update -g aks-rg -n prod --attach-acr myacr
az acr task create -r myacr -n build-web --image web:{{.Run.ID}} --context https://<git-url> --file Dockerfile --commit-trigger-enabled false
tip: Turn on content trust or use Notation signing and Defender for Containers scanning to complete the supply chain story.
a: Azure Container Registry stores OCI images and Helm charts. With the Premium SKU I can enable geo-replication, so one registry name serves images from replicas in several regions, which speeds up pulls for regional clusters, reduces data transfer and keeps working if a region has trouble. ACR Tasks run builds, tests and base image updates inside Azure, triggered by commits or base image changes, which helps keep images patched. For authentication, AKS clusters use the kubelet's managed identity, which is granted the AcrPull role on the registry, set with the attach-acr option, so no pull secrets are stored. To lock it down I use private endpoints, disable the admin account, restrict public network access, enable vulnerability scanning with Defender, sign images, and use retention policies to delete old tags and untagged manifests so storage costs stay under control.

How do you automate base image patching?

q: What is node auto-provisioning (Karpenter) on AKS, and how is it different from the Cluster Autoscaler?
p: The Cluster Autoscaler scales pre-defined node pools, each with one VM size. Node auto-provisioning, built on Karpenter, picks VM sizes dynamically for pending pods and consolidates nodes, reducing pool sprawl and wasted capacity.
cmds: az aks update -g aks-rg -n prod --node-provisioning-mode Auto
kubectl get nodepools.karpenter.sh
kubectl get nodeclaims
tip: Define limits on each NodePool so a runaway deployment cannot provision unlimited nodes.
a: The Cluster Autoscaler works on node pools that you define in advance. Each pool uses a fixed VM size, so to support different pod shapes you create many pools, and scale-up picks a pool rather than the best size. Node auto-provisioning is AKS's managed Karpenter. You declare constraints in NodePool and node class resources, such as allowed VM families, architectures, zones, Spot or on-demand and CPU and memory limits. When pods are pending, it chooses the cheapest suitable VM size that fits them, launches it directly, and later consolidates by replacing underused nodes with fewer or smaller ones. This often improves bin packing and reduces cost, and removes the need to manage many pools. Considerations are setting limits, using disruption budgets to control consolidation, keeping a small system pool, and understanding that some features of classic pools may not be available.

q: Explain Blob access tiers, lifecycle management and immutability for compliance data.
p: Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive trade lower storage cost for higher access cost and retrieval delay. Lifecycle rules move or delete blobs by age. Immutable storage with legal hold or time-based retention makes blobs WORM, so they cannot be altered or deleted.
cmds: az storage account management-policy create --account-name stlogs -g data-rg --policy @lifecycle.json
az storage container immutability-policy create --account-name stlogs -c audit --period 365
az storage blob set-tier --account-name stlogs -c logs -n 2026/10/a.log --tier Archive
tip: Archive blobs need rehydration, which can take hours, so never put data there that incident response might need quickly.
a: Storage tiers let me match cost to access patterns. Hot has higher storage cost and lowest access cost, Cool and Cold are cheaper to store but charge more to read and have minimum retention days, and Archive is offline, cheapest to store, but needs rehydration that can take hours. Lifecycle management policies automate transitions based on last modified or last accessed time and can delete after a retention period, so I define them as code per container prefix. For compliance data such as audit logs or financial records, immutable storage provides write once read many behaviour. A time-based retention policy prevents modification or deletion until the period ends, and a legal hold blocks changes until removed. A locked policy cannot be shortened, so I test with an unlocked policy first. I also enable versioning, soft delete and geo-redundancy for important data.

q: Azure Files versus Azure NetApp Files versus Blob for shared storage on AKS and VMs.
p: Azure Files offers managed SMB and NFS shares and is the easy default. NetApp Files delivers high-performance, low-latency NFS and SMB with enterprise features at higher cost. Blob is object storage, mounted via blobfuse for read-heavy use but not a general POSIX filesystem.
cmds: kubectl get storageclass
kubectl apply -f pvc-azurefile.yaml  # storageClassName: azurefile-csi-premium
az netappfiles volume list -g data-rg --account-name anf --pool-name pool1 -o table
tip: Say that RWX volumes on AKS are typically Azure Files or NetApp Files, while Azure Disk is single-attach RWO.
a: Azure Files provides fully managed file shares over SMB and NFS, integrates with the Azure Files CSI driver for ReadWriteMany volumes on AKS, supports snapshots and backup, and has standard and premium performance. It is the right default for shared configuration, content or moderate workloads. Azure NetApp Files is built on NetApp hardware, giving very low latency, high throughput and fine-grained performance tiers, which suits databases like SAP HANA, HPC and heavy shared workloads, at a higher price and with capacity pool minimums. Blob storage is object storage with a flat namespace, ideal for data lakes, media and backups. It can be mounted with blobfuse or the NFS feature, but semantics and latency differ from a true file system, so I avoid it for applications needing POSIX behaviour or many small writes. For single-pod block storage with the best IOPS, I use Azure Disk.

When is premium Files worth it?

q: Shared access signatures versus Entra ID authorisation for Azure Storage: which should you use?
p: Entra ID with RBAC is the preferred method: identity-based, auditable, revocable, no secrets. SAS tokens are bearer URLs for delegated, time-limited access. User delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials and is safer than account-key SAS. Disable shared key access where possible.
cmds: az storage blob generate-sas --account-name stapp -c files -n report.pdf --permissions r --expiry 2026-10-21T18:00Z --as-user --auth-mode login
az storage account update -n stapp -g data-rg --allow-shared-key-access false
az role assignment create --assignee <id> --role 'Storage Blob Data Contributor' --scope <storage-id>
tip: Account-key SAS cannot be revoked individually, so rotating the key is the only emergency stop. Use stored access policies or user delegation SAS.
a: For applications and people inside my tenant, I use Entra ID authentication with Azure RBAC data roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader. It uses managed identities, produces identity-based logs, supports Conditional Access and needs no stored secrets. A shared access signature is a URL with a token that grants specific permissions on specific resources for a limited time, which is ideal for giving an external client or a browser upload access without an Azure identity. There are three types: account SAS and service SAS, signed with the storage account key, and user delegation SAS, signed with Entra credentials, which is more secure and what I prefer. Account keys give full control and cannot be selectively revoked, so for production I disable shared key access, rotate keys if exposed, keep SAS expiry short, restrict by IP and protocol, and monitor access logs.

q: Explain the five Cosmos DB consistency levels and how you choose between them.
p: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix and Eventual trade consistency for latency, availability and throughput. Session is the default and a good fit for most apps because each client reads its own writes.
cmds: az cosmosdb update -g data-rg -n cosmos-prod --default-consistency-level Session
az cosmosdb show -g data-rg -n cosmos-prod --query consistencyPolicy
tip: Strong consistency is not available across multiple write regions, and it costs more RUs for reads. Know both caveats.
a: Cosmos DB offers five levels along a spectrum. Strong gives linearizable reads, always seeing the latest committed write, but with higher latency and reduced availability across regions. Bounded Staleness guarantees reads lag behind writes by at most a set number of versions or a time interval, giving predictable ordering with global distribution. Session, the default, guarantees that within a client session you read your own writes and see monotonic reads, which satisfies most application needs at low cost. Consistent Prefix ensures reads never see out-of-order writes but may be stale. Eventual gives the lowest latency and highest availability, with no ordering guarantee. I start with Session, move to Bounded Staleness when a defined freshness matters across regions, and use Strong only for cases like financial balances where the latency is acceptable. Clients can also relax the account level per request.

q: Azure SQL elastic pools, serverless and Hyperscale: when does each fit?
p: Elastic pools share resources across many databases with uneven usage. Serverless auto-scales compute and can pause when idle, billing per second. Hyperscale separates compute and storage for very large databases up to 100 TB with fast scale and restores.
cmds: az sql elastic-pool create -g data-rg -s sql-prod -n pool1 --edition GeneralPurpose --family Gen5 --capacity 8
az sql db create -g data-rg -s sql-prod -n reports --edition GeneralPurpose --compute-model Serverless --auto-pause-delay 60
az sql db update -g data-rg -s sql-prod -n big --service-objective HS_Gen5_8
tip: Serverless suits dev, test and intermittent workloads. The first query after auto-pause is slow because the database must resume.
a: These solve different problems. An elastic pool gives a shared pool of CPU and storage to many databases whose peaks do not coincide, such as a database per tenant in a SaaS product, so I pay for the pool rather than for the sum of individual peaks. Serverless is a compute tier for single databases that automatically scales between minimum and maximum vCores based on load, bills per second, and can pause after an idle delay, so it is good for development, test or sporadic workloads, though resume takes time. Hyperscale uses a distributed architecture with page servers and log service, allowing storage up to a hundred terabytes, fast scale up and out, near instant backups and quick restores regardless of size, plus multiple named read replicas. I choose Hyperscale for large or fast-growing databases, pools for multi-tenant estates, and General Purpose or Business Critical for steady OLTP.

q: How does high availability work for Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, and what does a failover look like?
p: Zone-redundant HA keeps a standby in another availability zone with synchronous replication, and automatic failover promotes it, usually within one to two minutes, keeping the same connection string. Same-zone HA protects against server failure only.
cmds: az postgres flexible-server update -g data-rg -n pg-prod --high-availability ZoneRedundant --standby-zone 2
az postgres flexible-server restart -g data-rg -n pg-prod --failover Forced
az postgres flexible-server show -g data-rg -n pg-prod --query highAvailability
tip: Test with a forced failover in a non-production server so your connection retry logic is proven.
a: With high availability enabled on a Flexible Server, Azure maintains a standby replica and replicates changes synchronously, so a committed transaction exists on both. In zone-redundant mode, the standby is in a different availability zone, protecting against zone failure, and in same-zone mode it is in the same zone, protecting against host or server failure. If the primary becomes unhealthy, or during some maintenance events, the service fails over automatically by promoting the standby and updating DNS, so the connection string stays the same. Applications see dropped connections for roughly a minute or two, so they must retry with backoff and re-resolve DNS. HA does not protect against human error or corruption, so I also rely on automated backups with point-in-time restore, and use read replicas for read scaling and cross-region disaster recovery.

q: How do Application Insights sampling and distributed tracing work, and how do you control telemetry cost?
p: Application Insights collects requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces, correlated by operation ID. Adaptive sampling keeps a percentage of telemetry, preserving related items together, which cuts ingestion while still giving accurate counts. Distributed tracing uses W3C trace context.
cmds: requests | where success == false | summarize count() by resultCode, bin(timestamp, 5m)
dependencies | where duration > 2000 | summarize avg(duration) by target
az monitor app-insights component show -g mon-rg -a web-ai --query samplingPercentage
tip: Sample requests and dependencies, but never sample away exceptions you rely on for alerting without checking the config.
a: Application Insights instruments an application with an SDK or auto-instrumentation and sends requests, dependency calls, exceptions, custom events and traces to a Log Analytics workspace. Each item carries an operation ID, so the end-to-end transaction view can show a request flowing through multiple services, using the W3C trace context headers to propagate identity across HTTP calls and messages. Since volume drives cost, sampling is the main control. Adaptive sampling automatically reduces the rate when traffic is high, and it keeps related telemetry for the same operation together, with the sampling percentage stored so metrics can be adjusted. I can also use fixed rate or ingestion sampling, filter out noisy health check requests, limit custom dimensions, set a daily cap as a safety valve, and send high-volume logs to cheaper table plans. I align this with OpenTelemetry where possible for portability.
f: Why is adaptive sampling better than random drop?
How do you correlate logs with traces?

q: How do you design a Log Analytics workspace strategy: one or many, retention, and table plans?
p: Start with a small number of workspaces split by region, compliance and access boundaries, not by team. Set retention per table, use Basic or Auxiliary table plans for high-volume low-value logs, and use data collection rules to filter before ingestion.
cmds: az monitor log-analytics workspace create -g mon-rg -n law-prod --retention-time 90
az monitor log-analytics workspace table update -g mon-rg --workspace-name law-prod -n ContainerLogV2 --plan Basic
az monitor log-analytics workspace data-export create -g mon-rg --workspace-name law-prod -n archive --tables AuditLogs --destination <storage-id>
tip: Table-level RBAC and resource-context access let teams see only their own logs inside a shared workspace.
a: I prefer few workspaces, because cross-workspace queries are more complex and alerts and dashboards are easier in one place. I split only when needed: data residency by region, strict separation of security and operations data, different retention or ownership, or billing needs. Within a workspace, access can be managed using resource-context RBAC, so a team that has access to its own resources sees only their logs, and table-level RBAC for sensitive tables. For cost I set retention per table, with interactive retention for recent data and long-term retention or archive for compliance, choose the Basic or Auxiliary plans for verbose, rarely queried logs such as container stdout, use data collection rules to filter and transform before ingestion, use commitment tiers when daily volume is large, and export to storage for cheap long-term archive. I monitor ingestion per table and set alerts on spikes.
