q: Metric alerts, log search alerts and dynamic thresholds in Azure Monitor: when do you use each?
p: Metric alerts are near real-time and cheap, evaluated on platform or custom metrics. Log search alerts run a KQL query on a schedule and handle complex conditions. Dynamic thresholds learn normal behaviour so you avoid hand-tuned numbers.
cmds: az monitor metrics alert create -n high-cpu -g mon-rg --scopes <vm-id> --condition 'avg Percentage CPU > 85' --window-size 5m --evaluation-frequency 1m --action <action-group-id>
az monitor scheduled-query create -n errors -g mon-rg --scopes <law-id> --condition 'count > 10' --condition-query 'AppExceptions | where TimeGenerated > ago(5m)'
tip: Route alerts through action groups, and use alert processing rules to suppress them during planned maintenance.
a: Metric alerts evaluate numeric time series, such as CPU or request latency, as often as every minute, support multiple dimensions, and are inexpensive and fast, so I use them for core health signals. Log search alerts run a KQL query against Log Analytics or Application Insights on a schedule, which allows complex conditions like error rates by customer, absence of heartbeats, or correlations across tables, but they have more latency and cost per evaluation. Dynamic thresholds apply machine learning to a metric's history, accounting for daily and weekly patterns, and alert on deviations, which suits metrics without a fixed good value. Alerts fire to action groups that notify people, call webhooks, run automation or open tickets. I scope them with tags, use severity levels, add alert processing rules for maintenance windows, and prefer symptom-based alerts over cause-based ones.
f: What do action groups contain?
How would you alert on a missing heartbeat?

q: How do Azure DevOps service connections use workload identity federation instead of secrets?
p: A service connection can use an app registration or managed identity with a federated credential that trusts the Azure DevOps issuer and subject. Pipelines get short-lived tokens, so no client secret is stored or needs rotation.
cmds: az ad app federated-credential create --id <app-id> --parameters @fedcred.json
az role assignment create --assignee <app-id> --role Contributor --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/app-rg
az devops service-endpoint list -o table
tip: Scope the identity's role to a resource group per environment, and use environment approvals for production service connections.
a: Traditionally, service connections used a service principal with a client secret that was stored in Azure DevOps, expired every year or two, and could leak. With workload identity federation, I create an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity and add a federated credential that trusts Azure DevOps as an issuer for a specific organization, project and service connection subject. When a pipeline runs, Azure DevOps issues a signed token for that job, which Entra ID exchanges for a short-lived access token, so there is nothing to store, rotate or steal. I grant the identity the minimum RBAC role at the narrowest scope, use separate connections per environment, require approvals and checks on production, and restrict which pipelines can use each connection. The same pattern applies to GitHub Actions with OIDC.
f: What is in the subject claim?
How do you restrict which pipelines use the connection?

q: How do App Service deployment slots enable zero-downtime releases and fast rollback?
p: A slot is a live app with its own hostname and settings. You deploy to staging, warm it up, then swap, which redirects production traffic to the already running instance. Swapping back is an instant rollback. Slot-sticky settings stay with the slot.
cmds: az webapp deployment slot create -g app-rg -n web --slot staging
az webapp deploy -g app-rg -n web --slot staging --src-path app.zip
az webapp deployment slot swap -g app-rg -n web --slot staging --target-slot production
tip: Use swap with preview or auto-swap warm-up to avoid sending users to a cold instance, and mark connection strings that differ as slot settings.
a: Deployment slots are full app instances that share the same App Service plan, each with its own URL and configuration. I deploy a new build to a staging slot, run smoke tests there, and let the swap operation warm up the instances by sending requests to the configured paths. Then the swap exchanges the routing so that the warmed instances take production traffic, with no cold start or downtime. If problems appear, swapping again restores the previous version immediately, because the old code is still running in the other slot. Settings can be marked as slot-specific so that, for instance, production keeps its own database connection string. I can also route a small percentage of traffic to a slot for canary testing. Considerations are that slots share plan resources, background jobs may run in both slots, and database changes need to be backward compatible.
f: Which settings should be sticky?
How does swap with preview work?

q: How do Azure DevOps environments, approvals and checks protect production deployments?
p: An environment represents a deployment target. Approvals, branch controls, exclusive locks and business-hour checks can be attached to it, so a pipeline stage targeting that environment pauses until all checks pass, regardless of who edits the YAML.
cmds: az devops invoke --area distributedtask --resource environments --route-parameters project=app --api-version 7.1
az pipelines run --name deploy-prod --branch main
tip: Put checks on the environment and service connection, not only in pipeline YAML, because anyone who can edit YAML can remove YAML-based gates.
a: In Azure Pipelines, a deployment job targets an environment, such as staging or production. Protections are configured on the environment resource itself, not in the pipeline file. I add manual approvals from a specific group, with a timeout, branch control so only the main branch can deploy, an exclusive lock so one deployment runs at a time, invoke Azure Function or REST API checks to validate change tickets or monitoring status, and business-hours restrictions. I also apply checks on the service connection and variable groups, so a pipeline cannot reach production secrets without passing them. Because the checks sit outside of YAML, a developer editing the pipeline cannot bypass them. Combined with required reviewers on pull requests and artifact promotion rather than rebuilding, this gives an auditable path to production, and deployment history on the environment helps with traceability.
f: Why not put approvals only in YAML?
What is an exclusive lock?

q: What are VM Scale Set orchestration modes, and how do Flexible and Uniform differ?
p: Flexible orchestration lets you mix VM sizes and manage VMs like standalone VMs inside a scale set, with spread across zones and fault domains. Uniform manages identical instances from one model, with simpler autoscaling. Flexible is now recommended for new designs.
cmds: az vmss create -g app-rg -n web-vmss --orchestration-mode Flexible --image Ubuntu2204 --zones 1 2 3 --instance-count 3
az monitor autoscale create -g app-rg --resource web-vmss --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets --min-count 3 --max-count 12 --count 3
tip: Mention that AKS node pools are VM scale sets under the hood, so scale set concepts explain AKS behaviour.
a: A virtual machine scale set manages a group of VMs for scaling and availability. In Uniform orchestration, all instances are created from one scale set model, are treated as identical, and are managed through the scale set API, which is simple for stateless fleets. Flexible orchestration is the newer model: VMs behave more like regular Azure VMs that happen to be in a group, you can mix sizes and Spot with on-demand through instance mix, spread them across zones and fault domains with a fault domain count of your choice, and use standard VM APIs, networking and extensions. Flexible also integrates with Azure Compute Gallery images and works well for stateful or heterogeneous applications. Autoscale rules based on metrics or schedules adjust capacity, with cool-down periods to avoid flapping. I choose Flexible for new deployments unless a feature depends on Uniform.
f: How do instance mixing and Spot work together?
What are fault domains?

q: App Service, Azure Container Apps and AKS: how do you decide between them for a web API?
p: App Service is the simplest PaaS for web apps. Container Apps is serverless containers with KEDA scaling and Dapr, no cluster management. AKS gives the full Kubernetes API, custom networking and operators, but you run the platform.
cmds: az containerapp create -g app-rg -n api --environment cae --image myacr.azurecr.io/api:1.0 --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 20 --ingress external --target-port 8080
az webapp up -n web-api --runtime PYTHON:3.12
tip: Choose the least complex platform that meets requirements, and migrate up to AKS only when you truly need Kubernetes features.
a: I decide based on how much control I need versus how much operational work I accept. App Service is the easiest: deploy code or a container, with built-in TLS, slots, autoscale and authentication, and it fits conventional web apps and APIs. Container Apps runs containers on a managed Kubernetes-based platform without exposing it, with scale to zero, event-driven scaling through KEDA, revisions with traffic splitting, and Dapr for microservice patterns, which suits event-driven and microservice workloads of moderate complexity. AKS provides the full Kubernetes API, custom controllers and operators, service meshes, advanced scheduling and networking, and multi-tenant platform building, at the cost of cluster operations and a steeper skill requirement. Team size and skills matter. Most teams start on App Service or Container Apps, and choose AKS when they need Kubernetes-specific capabilities or an internal platform for many teams.
f: What can't Container Apps do that AKS can?
How do revisions help in Container Apps?

q: How do Azure Hybrid Benefit and reservations stack, and where do they apply?
p: Hybrid Benefit lets you use existing Windows Server, SQL Server or Linux subscriptions licences on Azure to remove the licence cost from the price. Reservations or savings plans then discount the compute. The two can be combined for the deepest savings.
cmds: az vm update -g app-rg -n win1 --license-type Windows_Server
az sql db update -g data-rg -s sql-prod -n orders --license-type BasePrice
az consumption reservation summary list --grain monthly --reservation-order-id <id>
tip: Check licence compliance and Software Assurance eligibility before enabling the benefit across a fleet.
a: Hybrid Benefit lets organisations with Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions apply their existing Windows Server, SQL Server, and certain Linux licences to Azure resources, so they pay only for the base compute rate instead of paying for the licence again. It applies to virtual machines, Azure SQL, SQL Managed Instance, AKS Windows nodes and others, and can be turned on with a licence type setting. Reservations and savings plans give a discount on the compute portion in exchange for a one or three year commitment. Since one removes the licence charge and the other lowers the compute rate, they stack, which can cut Windows or SQL workloads by a large margin. The caveats are licence compliance, tracking core counts and eligibility, and committing only to steady baseline capacity. I use Azure Advisor and cost analysis to find candidates, and a policy or script to audit licence settings.
f: What is the difference between reservations and savings plans?
How would you audit licence settings?

q: An AKS node pool fails to scale up with errors about quota or SKU availability. How do you resolve it?
p: Read the scale set or cluster autoscaler error. QuotaExceeded means regional vCPU or VM-family quota is full, so request an increase. SkuNotAvailable or AllocationFailed means the zone has no capacity, so use another size, zone or region.
cmds: az vm list-usage -l westeurope -o table | grep -i 'DSv5\|Total Regional'
az vm list-skus -l westeurope --size Standard_D8s_v5 --zone -o table
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler | grep -i fail
tip: Add multiple VM sizes across node pools, or use node auto-provisioning, to reduce dependence on one SKU.
a: I start with the exact error, found in the autoscaler logs, the activity log and the scale set events. If it says quota exceeded, either total regional vCPUs or the specific VM family quota is at the limit, so I check usage with the quota commands and request an increase, which can take time, while freeing capacity by removing unused resources. If it says the SKU is not available or allocation failed, the chosen zone or region lacks capacity or the size is restricted for my subscription. Then I try a different size, an additional node pool with another family, other zones, or a different region for new capacity. Long term I avoid depending on a single VM size by allowing several in node auto-provisioning or multiple pools with the autoscaler priority expander, pre-request quota ahead of launches, and monitor quota usage with alerts.
f: What is the priority expander?
How do you plan quota for a launch?

q: Front Door returns 503 errors or reports all origins unhealthy. How do you troubleshoot?
p: Check origin health probe results, probe path, protocol and expected status, then the origin's own availability and access restrictions, private link approvals, host header and certificate name, and whether the backend only accepts the Front Door ID.
cmds: az afd origin-group show -g edge-rg --profile-name global -n og1 --query healthProbeSettings
curl -v -H 'Host: app.contoso.com' https://<origin-fqdn>/health
az afd origin show -g edge-rg --profile-name global --origin-group-name og1 -n origin1
tip: Probes come from many edge IPs, so aggressive WAF or IP restrictions on the origin frequently cause false unhealthy status.
a: First I look at the origin group health in the metrics and the probe settings: path, protocol, interval and the success codes. A probe path that returns a redirect, authentication error or heavy response can mark healthy origins as unhealthy. Then I test the origin directly with curl using the same host header, checking certificate name mismatches, since Front Door validates the certificate against the origin host name. If the origin uses Private Link, I confirm the private endpoint connection was approved. I check network restrictions: the origin must allow the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and validate the X-Azure-FDID header, and WAF or rate limits must not block probe traffic. I also review routing rules and caching, which can serve errors. Once fixed, I reduce probe cost by using a lightweight endpoint, and add alerts on origin health percentage.
f: Why do probes come from many IPs?
What is the X-Azure-FDID header?

q: AKS pods get ErrImagePull from Azure Container Registry with an unauthorized error. What do you check?
p: The kubelet identity probably lacks AcrPull on the registry, the registry is behind a firewall or private endpoint the nodes cannot reach, or the image reference is wrong. Verify with az aks check-acr and the pod events.
cmds: az aks check-acr -g aks-rg -n prod --acr myacr.azurecr.io
az role assignment list --assignee $(az aks show -g aks-rg -n prod --query identityProfile.kubeletidentity.objectId -o tsv) --scope <acr-id>

kubectl describe pod

| tail -15
tip: After switching to a private registry endpoint, make sure the private DNS zone is linked to the cluster's VNet.
a: The pod events give the real error. For unauthorized or authentication required, the kubelet's managed identity probably does not have the AcrPull role on the registry, which can happen when a cluster is created without attach-acr or when the registry is in another subscription. The az aks check-acr command validates DNS resolution, network reachability and authentication from inside the cluster. If the error is a timeout or name resolution failure, the registry may have a firewall or private endpoint, and the nodes cannot reach it or the private DNS zone is not linked to the node VNet. I also verify the image name, tag and registry login server, since typos are frequent, and whether the tag exists. For images from other registries I use pull secrets. Fixes are granting AcrPull, correcting network rules or DNS, and then deleting the failing pods so they retry.
f: What does attach-acr do?
How do you debug private DNS for ACR?

q: kubectl cannot reach a private AKS cluster, or stops working after enabling API server authorised IP ranges. How do you fix access?
p: A private cluster exposes the API server only on a private IP, so you must connect from the VNet, a peered network, VPN, or use az aks command invoke. For authorised ranges, add your egress IP and mind NAT changes.
cmds: az aks command invoke -g aks-rg -n prod --command 'kubectl get nodes'
az aks update -g aks-rg -n prod --api-server-authorized-ip-ranges 203.0.113.10/32,198.51.100.0/24
nslookup prod-dns-abc.privatelink.westeurope.azmk8s.io
tip: Command invoke is the escape hatch when you lock yourself out, but only if you still have RBAC rights on the cluster resource.
a: With a private cluster the API server has no public endpoint, so my client must be in the VNet, in a peered VNet, on a VPN or ExpressRoute connection, or on a jump host or build agent inside the network, and it must resolve the private DNS zone for the API server name. If DNS fails, the zone is probably not linked to my network or custom DNS servers do not forward the privatelink zone. For public clusters with authorised IP ranges, requests from outside the list are rejected, so I add the current egress IPs of engineers and CI systems, remembering that NAT gateways or proxies change the visible address. As a workaround I can run commands through az aks command invoke, which executes inside the cluster via the Azure control plane. For CI, I use self-hosted agents inside the network, and document the connectivity design.
f: How does az aks command invoke work?
What DNS zone does a private AKS cluster use?

q: A pod cannot mount an Azure Disk because of a zone mismatch or attach error. How do you diagnose it?
p: Azure Disks are zonal and attach to one node. A disk in zone 1 cannot attach to a node in zone 2, and a disk still attached to a failed node blocks reattachment. Check the PV node affinity, pod events, and the VMSS disk attachment.
cmds:
kubectl describe pod

| grep -i -A3 'attach\|volume'
kubectl get pv <pv> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeAffinity}'
az disk show -g MC_aks-rg_prod_westeurope -n <disk> --query '[zones,managedBy,diskState]'
tip: Use zone-redundant storage disks (ZRS) for stateful sets that must move across zones, and the WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode.
a: I read the events on the pod, which typically show a multi-attach error, a failed attach, or a message that the volume has node affinity conflicts. For zone problems, I compare the zone in the persistent volume's node affinity with the zones of available nodes. If all nodes in that zone are full or have been scaled away, the pod cannot be scheduled elsewhere. Solutions include ensuring there are nodes in each zone with enough capacity, using the WaitForFirstConsumer volume binding mode so the disk is created where the pod lands, and using ZRS disks, which can attach across zones. For attach errors after node failure, the disk may still be listed as attached to the old VM, and I check the disk's managedBy property and the VMSS instance state, and wait for detachment or detach it manually once the node is confirmed gone. Prevention involves PodDisruptionBudgets, node health alerts and backups.
f: What does ZRS on a managed disk do?
Why use WaitForFirstConsumer?

q: A pod gets 403 Forbidden from Azure Key Vault even though the identity looks correct. What do you check?
p: Confirm which authorisation model the vault uses (RBAC or access policies) and that the identity has the right role, then check the vault firewall and private endpoint rules, soft-delete state of the secret, and that the token is for the correct identity and audience.
cmds: az keyvault show -n kv-prod --query '{rbac:properties.enableRbacAuthorization,fw:properties.networkAcls}'
az role assignment list --assignee <client-id> --scope $(az keyvault show -n kv-prod --query id -o tsv)

kubectl logs

-c azwi-proxy
tip: The error message includes the caller's object ID. Compare it with the identity you expect.
a: The 403 message includes the principal's object ID, so I first verify that it is the identity I expect, since pods sometimes pick up a different identity than intended. Then I check the vault's permission model: if RBAC is enabled, the identity needs a role such as Key Vault Secrets User at the vault or secret scope, and old-style access policies are ignored, whereas with access policies the identity must be listed there. Next, I look at the network side: if the vault firewall is set to selected networks or private endpoint only, the cluster's outbound IP or subnet must be allowed, and DNS must resolve to the private IP. I also check that the secret is not deleted or disabled and that role assignments have propagated, which can take a few minutes. With Workload Identity I verify the federated credential subject and service account annotation, and with the CSI driver the SecretProviderClass settings.
f: RBAC versus access policies in Key Vault?
How does the Secrets Store CSI driver authenticate?

q: An Azure SQL database sits at 100% CPU or DTU and the app slows down. How do you find the cause and respond?
p: Use Query Performance Insight and Query Store to find top consuming queries, check missing indexes, plan regressions and blocking, then apply tuning. Scale up temporarily to relieve pressure while you fix the root cause.
cmds: SELECT TOP 10 qs.total_worker_time/qs.execution_count AS avg_cpu, st.text FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) st ORDER BY avg_cpu DESC;
SELECT * FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details;
az sql db update -g data-rg -s sql-prod -n orders --service-objective S6
tip: Scaling up is a stopgap and takes effect with a brief connection drop. Fix the query or index afterwards.
a: First I confirm what is saturated, whether CPU, data IO, log IO or workers, using the metrics and the resource utilisation views. Then I open Query Performance Insight or Query Store to see the top queries by CPU, duration and execution count, and check whether a recent deployment or plan change caused a regression. Common causes are missing or unused indexes, parameter sniffing, scans on large tables, chatty ORMs issuing thousands of small queries, and blocking or deadlocks. Quick relief is to scale the database up or enable read scale-out for reporting, which is done online with a short interruption. Then I fix the root cause: add or adjust indexes, rewrite queries, force a known good plan in Query Store, fix the N+1 pattern, and add caching. Automatic tuning can create and drop indexes, and I set up alerts on CPU percentage and long-running queries to catch it earlier next time.
f: What is parameter sniffing?
What does Query Store record?

q: A Cosmos DB container returns 429 errors under load. How do you fix throttling without overspending?
p: 429 means requests exceed provisioned RU/s on a partition or the container. Check normalised RU consumption per partition to see whether it is a hot key or overall load. Fix with better partition key, autoscale, indexing policy changes, query tuning and retry handling.
cmds: az cosmosdb sql container throughput update -g data-rg -a cosmos-prod -d appdb -n orders --max-throughput 20000
az monitor metrics list --resource <cosmos-id> --metric NormalizedRUConsumption --dimension PartitionKeyRangeId
SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.tenantId = @t
tip: Every query should include the partition key. Cross-partition fan-out queries burn RUs quickly.
a: A 429 status means the request rate exceeded the throughput available, measured in request units per second. I look at the normalised RU consumption metric split by partition key range. If a single partition is at one hundred percent while others are idle, it is a hot partition, and the fix is a better partition key or a synthetic key that spreads load. If all partitions are busy, the container needs more throughput, so I switch to autoscale, which scales between ten percent and the maximum, or raise the provisioned limit, while keeping an eye on cost. I also reduce RU consumption per operation: review indexing policy to exclude unused paths, make queries include the partition key, use point reads instead of queries, project fewer fields and use smaller documents. Clients should handle 429 with the SDK's retry-after logic, and I alert on throttled request counts.
f: What is a point read?
How does autoscale billing work?

q: Applications get 503 ServerBusy or throttling errors from an Azure Storage account. What do you do?
p: The account or a partition hit scalability targets for requests or bandwidth. Check metrics for throttled transactions and ingress or egress, spread load across blobs and prefixes, add retry with backoff, use premium tiers or multiple accounts, and add a CDN for reads.
cmds: az monitor metrics list --resource <storage-id> --metric Transactions --dimension ResponseType --interval PT1M
az storage account show -n stapp --query '{sku:sku.name,kind:kind}'
az storage blob list --account-name stapp -c data --prefix 2026/ --num-results 5
tip: Sequential naming such as timestamps in prefixes can concentrate load on a partition. Hash or reverse the prefix.
a: Each storage account and each partition has limits on requests per second and bandwidth. When we exceed them, the service responds with 503 server busy or 500 operation timeout. I look at the transaction metrics split by response type and API name to see which operations are throttled, and whether the limit hit was account-wide or on a particular blob prefix. Remedies include spreading load by using more diverse blob names, since the service partitions by name range, adding exponential backoff retries with the SDK, caching or putting Azure CDN or Front Door in front of read-heavy content, moving hot data to a premium block blob account for lower latency and higher transaction rates, and splitting workloads across multiple storage accounts. I also check for chatty clients making many small requests that could be batched. A request to Microsoft for higher account limits is possible for some cases.
f: Why do timestamp prefixes cause hot spots?
When would you use premium block blobs?

q: Log Analytics ingestion suddenly spiked and the bill jumped. How do you find the source and bring it down?
p: Query the Usage table by data type, resource and solution to find what grew. Typical causes are verbose container logs, debug logging, diagnostic settings sending all categories, or a loop. Filter at the source, change table plans and set a daily cap.
cmds: Usage | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | summarize GB = sum(Quantity)/1000 by DataType, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d) | order by GB desc
_BilledSize | summarize sum(_BilledSize) by _ResourceId | top 10 by sum_BilledSize
az monitor log-analytics workspace update -g mon-rg -n law-prod --quota 50
tip: The built-in Usage and Billing workbooks in Log Analytics show ingestion by table and resource without writing queries.
a: I begin with the Usage table, grouped by data type and day, to see which table grew and when. Then I drill down using the billed size column grouped by resource ID, namespace or computer to find the producer. Typical culprits are container stdout logs from a chatty or crash looping pod, an application with debug logging turned on, security events set to collect everything, diagnostic settings sending all categories from a busy resource, or a retry storm. Fixes depend on the source: reduce log levels, fix the loop, use data collection rules to filter or drop noisy records before ingestion, switch verbose tables to the Basic plan, shorten retention, or send low-value data to storage instead. A daily cap can protect the budget but causes data loss when reached, so I alert at lower thresholds first. I add an ingestion anomaly alert and review the top tables monthly.
f: What does the daily cap risk?
How do data collection rules reduce cost?

q: A Conditional Access policy locked administrators out of the tenant. How do you recover, and how do you prevent it?
p: Use emergency access (break-glass) accounts excluded from all Conditional Access policies, protected with strong credentials and monitored. Prevention is report-only mode first, exclusions, staged rollout and What If testing.
cmds: az ad user show --id breakglass1@contoso.onmicrosoft.com
az monitor activity-log list --offset 1h --query "[?contains(operationName.value,'conditionalAccess')]"
SigninLogs | where ConditionalAccessStatus == 'failure' | summarize count() by UserPrincipalName, tostring(ConditionalAccessPolicies)
tip: Alert on any sign-in by a break-glass account. It should happen almost never.
a: If a policy blocks all admins, for example by requiring a compliant device nobody has, recovery depends on having planned for it. Microsoft recommends at least two emergency access accounts that are cloud-only, use long random passwords or FIDO2 keys stored securely offline, are excluded from every Conditional Access policy, and have permanent Global Administrator rights. I sign in with one, review the sign-in logs to identify the policy and fix or disable it, then re-enable once verified. If no such account exists, recovery goes through Microsoft support, which is slow. To prevent the problem I always create new policies in report-only mode first and review the impact in the insights workbook, use the What If tool, roll out to a pilot group, avoid targeting all users and all apps together without exclusions, require change review, and alert on any use of break-glass accounts.
f: What is report-only mode?
Why must break-glass accounts avoid MFA dependencies on one method?

q: A pipeline suddenly fails because a service principal client secret expired. How do you fix it and remove the risk permanently?
p: Short term, create a new secret and update the service connection. Long term, move to workload identity federation or managed identities so there is no secret to expire, and alert on credential expiry for anything that remains.
cmds: az ad app credential list --id <app-id> --query '[].{id:keyId,end:endDateTime}'
az ad app credential reset --id <app-id> --years 1 --append
az devops service-endpoint list --query "[?authorization.scheme=='ServicePrincipal'].name"
tip: Ask who owns each service principal. Orphaned identities with no owner are the root of most expiry incidents.
a: The immediate fix is to create a new client secret for the app registration, store it in the secure place, update the service connection or variable, and re-run the pipeline. Using the append option avoids breaking consumers still on the old secret. Then I address the cause: secrets expire by design, and teams forget. I migrate service connections to workload identity federation, or to managed identities for self-hosted agents, so there is no secret at all. For any remaining secrets or certificates, I inventory them with a script or Microsoft Graph, record owners, set the shortest sensible lifetimes with automated rotation, and create alerts on expiry dates thirty and seven days ahead, using Key Vault expiry events or Azure Monitor queries. I also add ownership requirements to service principal creation and review them quarterly.
f: How do you rotate without downtime?
How can Key Vault events help?

q: A self-hosted Azure DevOps agent pool is offline and pipelines are queued. How do you troubleshoot and make agents resilient?
p: Check agent service status and logs, network access to dev.azure.com, expired PAT or authentication, disk space, and capacity limits. Make agents ephemeral using scale sets or Kubernetes so unhealthy ones are replaced automatically.
cmds: sudo ./svc.sh status
tail -n 50 _diag/Agent_*.log
az pipelines agent list --pool-id 12 -o table
df -h /home/vsts
tip: Scale set agents are recreated per job or on health failure, which removes drift and the usual full-disk problem.
a: First, I see whether the agent service is running on the machine and read the agent diagnostic logs. Common causes are the machine being down or out of disk space because of accumulated build workspaces and Docker layers, expired or revoked authentication tokens, an outbound proxy or firewall change blocking access to Azure DevOps endpoints, a version update that failed, or the pool having insufficient parallel jobs, which shows as queued rather than offline. I restart the service, free disk, renew credentials, or re-register the agent as needed. For resilience, I stop treating agents like pets: I use virtual machine scale set agent pools or agents running in Kubernetes, which are created from a clean image and removed after use, configured with minimum idle agents for responsiveness. I also add monitoring on queue time and agent count, and use Microsoft-hosted agents as a fallback where network access allows.
f: What is a scale set agent pool?
How do you control parallel job limits?

q: An App Service slot swap fails or sends users to a broken app. How do you recover and prevent it?
p: Swap back immediately to restore the previous version. Then check warm-up failures, slot-specific settings and connection strings, startup time, and incompatible database changes. Use swap with preview and health checks to catch issues before traffic moves.
cmds: az webapp deployment slot swap -g app-rg -n web --slot staging --target-slot production
az webapp config appsettings list -g app-rg -n web --slot staging
az webapp log tail -g app-rg -n web --slot staging
tip: Backward-compatible database migrations are what make a swap rollback safe. Otherwise, the old code meets the new schema.
a: If production is broken after a swap, the quickest recovery is to swap again, which puts the previous version back since it is still running in the other slot. Then I find out what went wrong. The swap warm-up may have failed because the application did not respond on the configured path or took too long to start, which can leave the target unwarmed. Settings might not have been marked as slot-specific, so staging values for connection strings or feature flags moved to production, or production settings did not apply. A database migration may have changed the schema in a way that old code cannot handle, which makes rollback unsafe. Prevention includes using swap with preview to test the staging slot with production settings first, configuring health checks and warm-up paths, marking sticky settings carefully, making migrations backward compatible, and running smoke tests automatically before and after the swap.
f: What does swap with preview do?
How do you make database changes rollback-safe?

q: A Bicep or ARM deployment fails halfway with RequestConflict or a resource lock error. How do you handle it?
p: Read the deployment operations for the failing resource and its correlation ID. Locks, in-progress operations, soft-deleted resources with the same name, and dependencies are common causes. Use what-if before deploying and make templates idempotent.
cmds: az deployment group what-if -g app-rg --template-file main.bicep --parameters env=prod
az deployment operation group list -g app-rg -n main --query "[?properties.provisioningState=='Failed']"
az lock list -g app-rg -o table
tip: Incremental mode adds and updates but does not delete resources. Complete mode deletes anything not in the template, so use it with extreme care.
a: I start with the deployment operations, which show which resource failed and the exact error and correlation ID. A resource lock on the group or resource returns a clear error, and I either remove the lock temporarily with authorisation or adjust the template. RequestConflict commonly means another operation on the same resource is still in progress, or that I'm trying to change an immutable property. Soft-deleted resources such as Key Vaults or Cognitive Services keep the name reserved, so I purge or recover them. Missing dependency order can be solved with references or explicit dependsOn. Before deployment I run what-if to preview the changes, validate the template, lint it, and deploy through a pipeline using incremental mode. Deployment stacks can manage the lifecycle and prevent drift. I also retry transient failures and keep templates idempotent so a rerun finishes the job.
f: Incremental versus complete mode?
What are deployment stacks?

q: Terraform on Azure fails with 'state blob is already locked'. What is going on and what is the safe fix?
p: The azurerm backend uses a blob lease as a lock. A previous run crashed or a pipeline was cancelled, leaving the lease, or another run is genuinely active. Confirm no apply is running before breaking the lease or using force-unlock.
cmds: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>
az storage blob show --account-name tfstate --container-name state --name prod.tfstate --query properties.lease
az storage blob lease break --account-name tfstate --container-name state --blob-name prod.tfstate
tip: Serialise pipelines per state file with concurrency groups so two applies cannot collide in the first place.
a: Terraform's azurerm backend stores state in a blob and locks it by taking a lease, so two runs cannot change the same state at once. This error means a lease is held. Either another run is genuinely in progress, or a previous run was killed, for instance a cancelled pipeline or a lost connection, before releasing it. The safe approach is to first check the pipelines and people to be sure no apply is running, because breaking the lock during a real apply can corrupt state. Then I use terraform force-unlock with the lock ID shown in the error, or break the lease on the blob. After unlocking, I run a plan to verify state matches reality, and if a partial apply occurred, I let Terraform reconcile or import missing resources. To prevent it I use pipeline concurrency controls per environment, avoid cancelling apply jobs, and enable blob versioning and soft delete on the state container.
f: Why enable versioning on the state container?
What happens if two applies run at once?

q: You cannot SSH or RDP to an Azure VM. What is your diagnostic order?
p: Check VM state and boot diagnostics, then network path: public IP or Bastion, NSG at subnet and NIC, effective routes, and guest firewall. Use IP flow verify, Run Command, serial console and the reset password or repair VM options.
cmds: az vm get-instance-view -g app-rg -n vm1 --query instanceView.statuses[].displayStatus
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g app-rg --vm vm1 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.0.1.4:22 --remote 203.0.113.5:50000
az vm run-command invoke -g app-rg -n vm1 --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'systemctl status sshd'
tip: Boot diagnostics screenshot and the serial console work even when the network is completely broken.
a: I move from outside in. First I make sure the VM is running and its health is fine, and look at the boot diagnostics screenshot and serial log for boot failures or a full disk. Then the network path: if I'm using a public IP, it exists and the NSG on the subnet and NIC allows my source IP on port 22 or 3389, and effective security rules and IP flow verify tell me exactly which rule blocks me. I check effective routes for a user-defined route sending traffic into a firewall that drops it, and whether just-in-time access needs a request. Inside the guest, the SSH daemon or Remote Desktop service may be stopped, the guest firewall may block, or credentials or keys may be wrong. Run Command, the serial console and the reset access extension help when the network path is fine but the guest is not. Bastion avoids many of these problems.
f: What does the serial console allow?
How does IP flow verify work?

q: ExpressRoute or VPN connectivity works one way or flaps after adding Azure Firewall. What could be wrong?
p: Asymmetric routing: return traffic takes a different path than the request, so the stateful firewall drops it. Check user-defined routes, BGP route propagation, gateway transit settings, and make both directions traverse the same appliance.
cmds: az network nic show-effective-route-table -g app-rg -n nic1 -o table
az network vnet-gateway list-learned-routes -g net-rg -n er-gw -o table
az network route-table route create -g net-rg --route-table-name spoke-rt -n to-onprem --address-prefix 10.200.0.0/16 --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance --next-hop-ip-address 10.0.1.4
tip: Draw the packet path for the request and the reply. If they differ, a stateful device in the middle will drop one of them.
a: When a stateful firewall sits in the path, it must see both directions of a flow. Asymmetric routing happens when the request goes through the firewall but the reply returns directly via the gateway, or the other way round, so the firewall never sees the full session and drops packets. I diagnose with effective routes on the VM network interface and on the gateway subnet, and learned and advertised BGP routes. Typical fixes are adding user-defined routes on the spoke subnets for the on-premises prefixes pointing to the firewall, and on the gateway subnet for spoke prefixes pointing to the firewall, disabling BGP route propagation on spoke route tables, and ensuring more specific routes do not bypass the firewall. Packet captures, connection monitor and firewall logs confirm the path. For flapping, I check BGP session timers, tunnel health, and MTU or MSS issues.
f: Why does a stateful firewall drop asymmetric flows?
What does BGP route propagation do?

q: The AKS cluster autoscaler does not scale down idle nodes. How do you find out why?
p: The autoscaler skips nodes it considers unsafe to remove: pods with local storage, restrictive PDBs, pods without controllers, annotations that block eviction, kube-system pods, or nodes below the utilisation threshold or within the cool-down. Read its status and logs.
cmds: kubectl get cm cluster-autoscaler-status -n kube-system -o yaml
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=cluster-autoscaler | grep -i 'scale-down\|not removable'
kubectl get pdb -A
tip: The annotation cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict=false pins a node, and forgotten annotations are a classic cause.
a: The autoscaler status ConfigMap and logs list why each candidate node was not removed. Reasons include pods that are not managed by a controller, pods using local storage or hostPath, pods with the safe-to-evict false annotation, a PodDisruptionBudget that would be violated, pods with strict affinity that cannot be placed elsewhere, system pods without a PDB, or node utilisation above the scale-down threshold of about fifty percent of requests. Timing settings also matter, since a node must be unneeded for around ten minutes after a scale-up before removal. I fix the cause by adding controllers, relaxing PDBs, moving local data to proper volumes, removing blocking annotations, and tuning profile settings such as scale-down utilisation threshold and delay after add. Over-requested resources make nodes look busy, so I also right-size pod requests.
f: How does utilisation threshold work?
What is the safe-to-evict annotation?

q: Spot node evictions are disrupting workloads on AKS. How do you design for them?
p: Spot capacity can be evicted with about 30 seconds notice. Use Spot only for interruptible work, spread across pools and sizes, keep a regular on-demand pool for critical pods, handle SIGTERM, use PDBs, retries and checkpointing, and set a max price strategy.
cmds: az aks nodepool add -g aks-rg --cluster-name prod -n spot1 --priority Spot --eviction-policy Delete --spot-max-price -1 --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 0 --max-count 20
kubectl taint nodes -l kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot:NoSchedule
tip: AKS taints Spot nodes by default, so workloads must opt in with a toleration. That keeps critical pods off by accident.
a: Azure Spot VMs use spare capacity at a steep discount, but Azure can evict them with roughly thirty seconds of notice when it needs the capacity back or when price exceeds your maximum. On AKS, Spot node pools are tainted by default so only pods that tolerate it run there. I put fault-tolerant work on them: stateless workers, batch jobs, CI runners, and replicas beyond the minimum that on-demand pools already cover. I design for interruption by handling SIGTERM and shutting down quickly, keeping jobs idempotent with checkpointing or queues for retry, using PodDisruptionBudgets and topology spread across several Spot pools with different VM sizes and zones to reduce simultaneous eviction, and listening for scheduled event notices. The user-facing baseline stays on a regular pool. I monitor eviction rates and compare real savings against the added complexity.
f: Why use several Spot pools with different sizes?
What is a Spot eviction policy?

q: After adding a user-defined route to Azure Firewall for egress control, new AKS nodes fail to join or pull images. What is missing?
p: AKS nodes need outbound access to required endpoints such as the Microsoft Container Registry, the API server, Azure management and package repositories. A firewall that blocks them breaks bootstrap. Allow the AzureKubernetesService FQDN tag and required network rules.
cmds: az network firewall application-rule create -g net-rg -f fw -c aks-rules -n aks-fqdn --source-addresses 10.1.0.0/16 --protocols http=80 https=443 --fqdn-tags AzureKubernetesService --priority 100 --action Allow
az aks show -g aks-rg -n prod --query 'networkProfile.outboundType'
kubectl get nodes
tip: Use the AzureKubernetesService FQDN tag so Microsoft maintains the required list for you.
a: With outbound type set to user-defined routing, all egress from the nodes goes to the firewall, so the firewall policy must allow what AKS needs to function. That includes the API server on port 443 and the tunnel connection, NTP, the Microsoft Container Registry and Azure management endpoints for image pulls, node image updates and monitoring, and OS package repositories. Missing any of these results in nodes stuck in NotReady, image pull failures or failed extensions. The simplest approach is an application rule using the AzureKubernetesService FQDN tag, which Microsoft keeps current, plus network rules for UDP 1194 or 9000 tunnel and NTP where applicable. I check firewall logs for denied requests from node IPs, and compare against Microsoft's documented egress requirements. I also add rules for my own registries and any monitoring endpoints, and test in a non-production cluster before rolling out egress restrictions.
f: What is an FQDN tag?
How do you read denied traffic in firewall logs?

q: A deployment fails with QuotaExceeded or 'not enough IP addresses in the subnet'. What are the fixes?
p: Check the regional vCPU quota and subnet free IPs. Request more quota, use a different size or region, or expand or add subnets. On AKS with Azure CNI each pod uses a VNet IP, so plan with CNI Overlay or dynamic IP allocation.
cmds: az vm list-usage -l westeurope -o table
az network vnet subnet show -g net-rg --vnet-name spoke1 -n aks --query '{prefix:addressPrefix,used:ipConfigurations|length(@)}'
az aks update -g aks-rg -n prod --network-plugin-mode overlay
tip: Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet, so a /24 gives 251 usable IPs.
a: For quota errors I list current usage against limits in the region and request an increase for the specific VM family or total regional vCPUs through the quota blade, as this can take time. As a workaround I deploy a different size or family, or use another region. For IP exhaustion the cause is subnet size: Azure reserves five addresses per subnet, and with traditional Azure CNI each pod consumes an address from the subnet, plus extra during upgrades, so large clusters drain a small subnet quickly. Remedies include moving to Azure CNI Overlay so pods use a private overlay range and only nodes use subnet addresses, using dynamic pod IP allocation with a separate pod subnet, adding larger subnets, or creating new node pools in a new subnet. Prevention comes from IP address planning at design time, tracking utilisation with alerts, and choosing a pod CIDR that does not overlap with on-premises networks.
f: Why does CNI Overlay save IPs?
How many IPs does Azure reserve per subnet?

q: A cost review finds orphaned disks, unused public IPs, old snapshots and idle gateways. How do you clean up safely and keep it clean?
p: Find candidates with Resource Graph queries and Advisor, confirm ownership and last use, snapshot or tag before deleting, and delete in stages. Prevent recurrence with tagging policies, lifecycle automation and budget alerts.
cmds: az graph query -q "Resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/disks' and isempty(managedBy) | project name, resourceGroup, sku.name, properties.diskSizeGB"
az graph query -q "Resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/publicipaddresses' and isnull(properties.ipConfiguration) | project name, resourceGroup"
az snapshot list --query "[?timeCreated<'2026-04-01'].name" -o tsv
tip: Tag resources with a pending-delete date and owner first, wait a notice period, then remove. Nobody gets surprised.
a: I use Azure Resource Graph to query across subscriptions for unattached managed disks, public IP addresses with no association, old snapshots, empty load balancers, idle VPN or application gateways, and stopped but not deallocated VMs, and combine the result with Advisor and cost analysis to prioritise by savings. Before deleting, I identify owners from tags or activity logs, notify them, and for data resources take a final snapshot or export. I tag candidates with a planned deletion date, wait for objections, and then delete in stages, starting with non-production. To keep things clean I enforce owner and expiry tags through Azure Policy, schedule recurring Resource Graph reports, automate shutdown of dev resources, use lifecycle rules on snapshots and backups, and run a monthly cost review. Dashboards by team make waste visible and create accountability.
f: What is Azure Resource Graph?
Deallocated versus stopped VMs?

q: Monthly cost for Application Gateway, Firewall and NAT in the hub is far higher than expected. How do you analyse and reduce it?
p: Break the bill down by meter. Fixed hourly charges for gateways and firewalls plus per-GB processing dominate. Right-size SKUs, consolidate instances, remove idle ones, reduce hairpin traffic, use Private Link and service endpoints, and move to Basic or Standard SKUs where features allow.
cmds: az costmanagement query --type ActualCost --scope /subscriptions/<sub> --timeframe MonthToDate --dataset-grouping name=MeterCategory type=Dimension
az network firewall show -g net-rg -n fw --query sku
AzureDiagnostics | where Category == 'AzureFirewallNetworkRule' | summarize bytes=sum(todouble(BytesTransferred)) by SourceIp | top 10 by bytes
tip: Check data processing meters. Large backups or replication traffic through a firewall can cost more than the firewall itself.
a: I use cost analysis grouped by meter to separate fixed deployment charges from data processing charges. Azure Firewall Premium, multiple Application Gateway instances with high minimum capacity, and several NAT or VPN gateways can quietly run into thousands per month. Reduction steps: delete idle or duplicate gateways, consolidate multiple application gateways using multi-site listeners, lower minimum autoscale counts, and choose the right SKU, for example Standard instead of Premium firewall if advanced inspection is not needed. For data processing, I find the top talkers with firewall logs and see whether bulk flows such as backups, replication or storage traffic can bypass inspection using private endpoints, service endpoints, or peering paths that don't need the firewall. I review regional data transfer and cross-zone traffic too. Reservations apply to some network services, and I document the security trade-offs of each change with the security team.
f: How do you find top talkers through the firewall?
When is Firewall Premium justified?
